titleText.es: Además, con todas las advertencias sobre rellenar completamente los círculos, me pasé como 30 segundos con cada uno.
titleText.en: Also, after all the warnings about filling in the bubbles completely, I spent like 30 seconds on each one.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely translates the official title text and preserves the numeral 30.

regions.labelEs: BIEN NIÑOS, HE ENTREGADO VUESTROS EXÁMENES PARA QUE LOS PUNTÚEN. AHORA-

applications.explanationEn: He is the present helper for the speaker, and entregado is the unchanged completed-action form.
Vuestros is the Spain-style informal plural possessive and matches the masculine plural thing owned.
Para que introduces the intended later event, los stands for the exams, and puntúen uses the special desired-result form.
Los replaces the masculine plural exámenes and appears directly before the changed verb puntúen.
The plural verb form points to unnamed people who will do the grading.

excludedUnits.rationale: LENHART is an unchanged personal surname, not a Spanish lexical word.

regions.labelEs: USÉ UN LÁPIZ Nº3 EN VEZ DE UNO Nº2. ¿AFECTA ESO EN ALGO?

excludedUnits.rationale: Nº3 is the printed numeric pencil-grade label, not a Spanish lexical word.
Nº2 is the printed numeric pencil-grade label, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: En vez de is the fixed substitution connector, and uno fills its alternative slot by standing for another pencil.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks for the surprising information to be repeated.
The two words form the fixed exclamation of shock.
The same two-word expression again marks an immediate shocked reaction.
Había is the past helper and visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver.

cards.noteEn: Niños can refer specifically to boys or more generally to a group of children whose members are male or mixed. The surrounding context decides which meaning is intended.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio.
example.en: The children are playing in the yard.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Entregado is the completed-action form of entregar. After a form of haber, it stays unchanged and can say that work, forms, or documents have been submitted.

example.en: I have submitted the report.

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural, before masculine plural things)

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.promptEs: hoja de respuestas óptica · lápiz n.º 2
cards.answerEn: A Scantron-style test records answers in filled bubbles that an optical mark reader can score; instructions have traditionally specified a No. 2 pencil.
cards.noteEn: Scantron still sells No. 2 pencils for optical-mark recognition, although current Scantron equipment can support pencil or ink depending on the form and scanner. The joke turns the minor choice of a No. 3 pencil into an absurdly violent grading disaster.

cards.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a purpose when someone or something else carries out the desired result?
cards.answerEn: Use para que, then put the result verb in the special form used for a purpose that is not yet a fact.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the second action is intended or desired, not presented as an established fact. For example, ordinary ve becomes vea, and ordinary viene becomes venga. Use para plus an unchanged action verb instead when the same person performs both actions.

example.es: Dejo una nota para que Ana la vea.
example.en: I leave a note so that Ana sees it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cards.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.answerEn: they grade; they score, as a desired result
cards.noteEn: Puntúen is a special form of puntuar used after para que because the grading is the intended next action, not a fact already being reported. The plural ending leaves the graders unnamed.

example.es: Envío las pruebas para que las puntúen.
example.en: I send the tests so that they can be graded.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de ellos/ellas sin agente nombrado
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish describe an action by unnamed people, where English might use a vague “they” or a passive sentence?
cards.answerEn: Use the plural “they” form of the verb and do not name who performed the action.
cards.noteEn: The plural verb ending points to people who did the action, but the speaker leaves them unidentified. Depending on the context, English may use “they,” “people,” “someone,” or a passive form such as “was built.” For a completed regular -ar action, the plural ending is -aron, as in llamaron.

example.en: The bridge was built in 1990.

cards.noteEn: Usé is the completed-past form of usar for the speaker. The written accent distinguishes this past form from the special present form use.

example.en: I used a blue pen.

cards.noteEn: Lápiz is singular. Its plural is lápices, with c instead of z.

example.es: Necesito un lápiz para el examen.
example.en: I need a pencil for the exam.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: En belongs to the fixed three-word connector en vez de. Learn the connector as a unit rather than translating en as ordinary ‘in.’

example.es: Tomé té en vez de café.
example.en: I had tea instead of coffee.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one option replaces another?
cards.answerEn: Put en vez de before the alternative that was not chosen: ‘instead of.’
cards.noteEn: A noun, pronoun, or unchanged action verb can follow: en vez de café, en vez de eso, en vez de llamar. The three words en vez de stay together.

example.es: Usamos el tren en vez del coche.
example.en: We used the train instead of the car.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; forms en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: Vez often means an occurrence or time, but inside en vez de it helps form the fixed connector ‘instead of.’

example.es: Fuimos andando en vez de tomar el autobús.
example.en: We walked instead of taking the bus.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: De finishes the connector en vez de and comes directly before the alternative that is not chosen.

example.es: Escribió un correo en vez de llamar.
example.en: She wrote an email instead of calling.

cards.noteEn: Uno can stand in for a masculine singular noun that has already been mentioned or is obvious from the situation, just as English can use ‘one.’

example.en: I need a pencil; give me one.

cards.answerEn: does it affect; does it make a difference
cards.noteEn: Afecta is a present form of afectar. In a question, it asks whether something changes the result or matters in some way. English adds ‘does’ before the subject, while the Spanish verb form stays afecta.

example.en: Does that affect the result?

cards.answerEn: in; in any way, as part of en algo
cards.noteEn: After a verb about changing or affecting something, en algo can ask whether there is any effect or difference at all.

example.en: Did the plan change in any way?

cards.noteEn: Algo refers to an unspecified thing. In a question, natural English often uses ‘anything’; after en, en algo can mean ‘in any way.’

example.en: Do you need anything?

cards.noteEn: Qué keeps its written accent in a short echo question. The speaker repeats only the missing or unbelievable information instead of forming a longer question.

example.en: ‘I'm leaving tomorrow.’ ‘What?’

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.noteEn: Aaaah stretches the vowel to write a scream or cry of alarm. The number of repeated letters varies with the imagined length of the sound.

example.en: Aaah! A spider!

cards.noteEn: Bam represents a loud, abrupt blow, collision, or impact in comics.

example.en: The door slammed shut: bam!

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’

example.en: Man, it's been so long!

cards.noteEn: Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.

example.en: My God! What happened?

cards.answerEn: had (helper for an earlier completed action)
cards.noteEn: Before a completed-action form such as escrito, había is a past form of the helper haber. It places one completed action before another point in the past.

example.en: I had already eaten when you called.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something had already happened before another past moment?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching past form of haber, then the action verb's completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: Use había for I, he, she, or one thing; habías for informal singular “you”; habíamos for “we”; habíais for informal plural “you” in Spain; and habían for “they” or plural formal “you.” The second verb uses a completed-action form, called a past participle: most -ar verbs end in -ado and most -er or -ir verbs end in -ido, although some are irregular, such as escribir → escrito. Only haber changes for the person; the completed-action form stays unchanged.

example.es: Ya habíamos terminado cuando llegó Luis.
example.en: We had already finished when Luis arrived.

cards.noteEn: Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

example.en: We have seen that movie.
